title: Lost updates: watch a race happen
summary: Why count++ on two threads can lose updates, seen one step at a time on real threads, and how to prove a fix holds for every interleaving.

steps.title: count++ is three steps, not one
body: `count++` looks like one operation. The CPU does it in three: **read** `count` into a register, **add** one, **write** the register back.
When two threads do that at the same time, the operating system can switch between them after any of those steps.
If both threads read before either writes, both write the same value and one increment is **lost**.
The card below runs this code for real: two threads, a scheduler that lets one thread move at a time, and a timeline like a profiler's.
Press **Play** to see the lucky order. Then pick **Lost update** under *Interleaving*, or click **Run next: T2** after T1's read and watch the register go stale.
Finally press **Try every interleaving**: it runs all of them and counts the results.

schedules.name: Lost update: both read before either writes

steps.prompt: In the card, four of the six interleavings end with `count = 1`. What do those four have in common?
options: Both threads read `count` before either of them writes it back
One of the threads never runs
The two writes happen at exactly the same time
explain: Each thread writes `(the value it read) + 1`. If both read 0, both write 1. Who goes first does not matter; what matters is that
the read of one thread falls between the read and the write of the other. That window is the **critical section**.

steps.prompt: Which of these are read-modify-write races when two threads run them on the same shared field, with no lock?
explain: Compound assignment (`+=`, `|=`) and indexer read-then-write are all read, compute, write. A check followed by an action
(`if (Count < 100) Add`) is the same shape: the check can be stale by the time the action runs. A local variable is private
to its thread, and `Interlocked.Increment` does the read, add and write as one atomic CPU instruction.

steps.title: Why your tests did not catch it
body: Run the racy counter with 2 threads and 1,000 increments each, and on most runs you get 2,000. The window between the read and the
write is a few nanoseconds, so it is rarely hit. Run it with a million increments on 8 cores and it is almost always wrong.
That is the danger: **a race passes in tests and fails in production**, under real load, a few times a day, with no stack trace.
Two ways to test concurrent code properly:
1. **Systematic exploration** (what the card does, and what tools like Microsoft's **Coyote** do for .NET): control the scheduler and
try every interleaving, or every one with a few forced switches. A bug that exists is found every time.
2. **Forced interleavings**: make the test itself pause one thread at the dangerous point (a `ManualResetEventSlim`, a `Barrier`,
a `TaskCompletionSource`), so the bad order happens on purpose. You will write these later in this module.
A stress test (many threads, many loops) is still useful as a smoke test, but a green stress run proves little.

steps.prompt: Match each step of `count++` to what it does on the CPU.
pairs: load the current value from memory into a register
change the register, which only this thread can see
store the register back to memory, overwriting what is there
a write that overwrites another thread's write it never saw

steps.prompt: Each thread does one `count++`, and they run in this order: T1 reads, T2 reads, T2 writes, T1 writes. What is `count` at the end? (It starts at 5.)
steps.explain: Both registers hold 5. T2 writes 6, then T1 writes 6 over it. Two increments ran and the value went up by one. The code above is exactly that interleaving, written out by hand.

steps.title: A lock makes the three steps one
body: `lock (gate) { ... }` lets only one thread at a time run the code inside. A second thread that reaches the `lock` **blocks** until the
first one leaves. The read, add and write can no longer be split by another thread's read.
In the card below, the threads take the lock first. Try to make T2 read early: the **Run next** button for T2 is disabled while it waits,
and its lane shows the red hatch for *blocked*. Then **Try every interleaving**: only one outcome is left.
```csharp
readonly Lock _gate = new();   // .NET 9+: System.Threading.Lock. Older code uses: readonly object _gate = new();
public void Record() { lock (_gate) { _total++; } }
Lock on a **private** object you own. `lock (this)` or `lock (typeof(X))` lets other code take your lock too, which invites deadlocks.

steps.prompt: Complete the counter so that `Record` is safe to call from many threads at once.
code: public int Total { get { lock (_gate) return _total; } }
steps.explain: Either `Lock` (the .NET 9+ type, slightly faster and clearer) or a plain `object` works with the `lock` statement. Reading `Total` inside the lock too guarantees you see the latest value.

steps.title: Make the hit counter safe for every interleaving
prompt: An API counts page hits with this class. Under load the totals come out low.
Fix `HitCounter` so that `Record()` never loses an update. Keep the names: `void Record()` and `int Total`.
**How it is checked:** the tests run two threads that each call `Record()` twice, under a scheduler that tries **every**
interleaving of their shared-memory steps (or every one with up to two forced switches, when there are too many). `Total`
must be 4 in all of them. If one breaks your code, the results show that exact interleaving on a timeline.
solution: public int Total { get { lock (_gate) return _total; } }
hints: Give the class a private object to lock on, and put the increment inside `lock (...) { }`.
`private readonly Lock _gate = new();` then `lock (_gate) { _total++; }`. `Interlocked.Increment(ref _total)` also works.
explain: Both fixes pass every interleaving. `Interlocked.Increment` is the cheapest for a single counter. A lock is the general tool: it
also protects several fields that must change together, which `Interlocked` cannot.
